subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students look at the picture of animals, birds, insects, and plants and discuss which ones live in their homes (p. 73)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 72–73 image of myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, and potted plants

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to look at the picture on Textbook pp. 72–73 quietly for a moment. Ask: 'Which of these have you seen near your home or inside it?' Let two or three students share briefly before framing the session's central question.

Whole-class discussion using the Textbook p. 73 prompts: Do any of these animals, birds, insects, and plants live with you? Do you and your family take care of them? Students share examples — invited guests like a pet cat or potted hibiscus, and uninvited visitors like a dragonfly or snail. Teacher listens and lists creatures on the board in two columns: 'Invited' and 'Arrived on their own'.

Students discuss in pairs: Which animals, birds, or insects visit their homes that are NOT shown in the picture on Textbook p. 72? Each pair talks about where they spotted these creatures — in the kitchen, the garden, on the wall, near a window. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Can you remember the name? Where exactly did you see it?'

Pairs share one creature each with the class. Teacher records names and locations on the board. Close by asking: 'Why do you think some animals choose to come into our homes even when we haven't invited them?' Accept responses warmly and leave the question open.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the animals, birds, insects, and plants that share their living space and explain why some arrive uninvited.
periods.section_context: Myna, hibiscus, dragonfly, cat, snail, goat, grasshopper, potted plants; invited vs. uninvited visitors; where animals were spotted at home.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students what their grandparents or older relatives say about animals that used to visit their homes — this opens intergenerational stories naturally. Keep the two-column board list visible throughout so the class can refer back to it.

periods.textbook_anchor: Living in Harmony — Students discuss how they feel about uninvited animals and what they do when they do not like them (p. 74)

time_bands.activity: Recap the two-column list from the previous discussion by asking the class to name a few uninvited creatures they recall. Then direct students to Textbook p. 74 and read the discussion prompts together: Which uninvited animals visit your home? Why do you think they come?

Small-group discussion (groups of four): students share stories about uninvited animals — a lizard on the wall, ants in the sugar tin, a crow on the windowsill. Groups discuss: Why might these creatures come inside? What do they need that our homes provide? Teacher circulates, listening and gently asking: 'Do you think they mean to bother us, or are they looking for something?'

Whole-class sharing on feelings and responses (Textbook p. 74 prompts): How do you feel about their presence? Which do you like? What do you do when you don't like them? Teacher draws out the range — curiosity, fear, affection, irritation — without judging any feeling. Guide reflection: Is there a kind way to respond even when we don't like a visitor?

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one naming an uninvited animal they don't like and why, and one describing a kind way they could respond to it. A few students share their sentences aloud. Teacher closes by affirming that caring for all living beings — even ones we don't love — is part of living in harmony.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate their feelings toward uninvited living beings and reflect on compassionate responses rather than harm.
periods.section_context: Uninvited animals, birds, and insects at home; feelings of like and dislike; reasons animals enter homes; kind vs. harmful responses.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family ever gently put an animal outside instead of hurting it? What did that feel like?' This surfaces the value of non-harm without stating it prescriptively. Ensure every feeling — including fear or dislike — is acknowledged before guiding toward compassion.

periods.activity_title: The Mango Tree and Its Many Guests
periods.textbook_anchor: The Mango Tree — Students discuss how plants help animals and how animals help plants, using the mango tree story and the uses-of-plants diagram (p. 77)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 75–77 uses-of-plants radial diagram (shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story of Shambhu and his father sitting under the mango tree aloud while students follow in their textbooks. Pause at the moment the father explains what happens when a monkey throws a mango seed. Ask: 'What do you think will happen to that seed?'

Students look at the uses-of-plants radial diagram on Textbook p. 77. Teacher goes through each spoke aloud — shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals. Students discuss in pairs: Which of these uses have you seen in your own life? Which plants give your family medicine, food, or shade?

Whole-class discussion using Textbook p. 77 prompts: How do plants help animals? How do animals help plants? How are we dependent on plants and animals? Students build a web of dependence on the board — teacher draws lines connecting humans, plants, and animals as students name connections (monkey spreads mango seeds; cow gives milk; tree gives shade to humans and shelter to birds).

Teacher poses the closing question: 'If every tree were cut down, what would happen to the animals that live in it, and what would happen to us?' Students respond briefly in pairs, then one or two share with the class. Teacher draws together the idea that the tree, its animal guests, and humans are all woven together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how plants and animals depend on each other and on humans, using examples from their own environment.
periods.section_context: Mango tree story; monkey and seed dispersal; uses-of-plants diagram (shade, wood, medicine, fibre, fruit, fresh air, shelter for animals); five-way interdependence between humans, plants, and animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students about trees in their neighbourhood — a neem, peepal, or coconut — and who or what lives in or uses that tree. This grounds the mango tree story in the children's own locality and naturally surfaces local ecological knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Get to Know an Animal — Close Observation
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students choose an animal they see often, observe it closely, and record its behaviour, movement, and sounds (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the 'Get to Know an Animal' activity from Textbook p. 78. Read the activity instructions together. Students choose one animal they see regularly — goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, or duck — and announce their choice to a partner. Teacher asks: 'Why that animal? Where do you usually see it?'

Teacher introduces the observation frame on the board: Name, Where I see it, Is it alone or with others?, How it moves, Sounds it makes, What it eats/does, Something surprising. Students open their notebooks and copy the frame. Teacher explains: 'You will use this frame whenever you observe your animal — in the schoolyard, at home, or on the way to school. Today we practise filling it from memory.'

Students fill in the observation frame from memory and imagination, drawing on what they already know about their chosen animal. Teacher circulates, prompting: 'Have you seen it sleeping? Fighting? Playing with others? Did it do anything that made you laugh?' Students who choose the same animal may compare notes quietly.

Three or four students share one surprising thing about their chosen animal with the class. Teacher closes by encouraging students to keep a bowl of water or some grain for their animal when they can, pointing to the suggestion on Textbook p. 78. Remind students that the observation frame in their notebook is theirs to add to whenever they notice something new.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a familiar animal closely and record its behaviour, movement, sounds, and social habits using a structured frame.
periods.section_context: Chosen animal (goat, cow, dog, cat, crow, pigeon, sparrow, parrot, duck); observation of behaviour, movement, sounds, feeding, social habits; bowl of water and grain as care practice.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family told you something about this animal that you didn't know before?' This invites intergenerational knowledge. If a student chooses an animal others do not know well, let them become the class expert on that creature.

periods.activity_title: Busy, Busy, Clever Ants — Predict and Observe
periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students place sweet, fried, and cooked food on the floor, make predictions, and observe ant behaviour and preferences (p. 79)
materials: Small amounts of sweet food (sugar or jaggery)
Small amounts of fried food (papad or murukku)
Small amounts of cooked food (bread, chapati, idli, rice, or ragi)
Three small plates or pieces of paper

time_bands.activity: Students read the 'Busy, Busy, Busy and Clever Ants!' activity on Textbook p. 79 together. Teacher displays the three food types (sweet, fried, cooked) and the eight prediction questions. Students write 'My Guess' answers in their notebooks for each question: Who will come? Which food will they prefer? Will they all look the same? How many will come? What will they do with the food?

Working in groups of five or six, students place the three food types on the floor with one foot between them (or on a low surface accessible and safe). Groups watch quietly and record what actually happens: which food attracted ants first, how many ants came to each, what the ants did with the food, whether all ants looked the same. Teacher circulates and asks: 'Is this what you predicted? What surprised you?'

Groups compare their predictions with their observations. Each group picks the one finding that surprised them most and prepares a one-sentence report. Teacher guides: 'Your observation is your evidence. What does it tell you about what ants prefer?'

Groups share their one surprising finding with the class. Teacher draws out the ecological connection: ants are always busy, they carry food back, they work together — connecting back to the chapter's theme that every creature has a role. Note the playful 'Do you know?' squirrel panel and the idea of animals accidentally helping the environment.

periods.implied_lo: Students can set up a simple inquiry, make predictions, record observations, and compare results to their predictions.
periods.section_context: Ant observation experiment; sweet food (sugar, jaggery), fried food (papad, murukku), cooked food (bread, chapati, idli, rice, ragi); eight prediction questions; ant behaviour, preferences, appearance, and food-carrying.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Before placing the food, ask: 'Where do you think the ants will come from? How do you think they know food is there?' This sharpens prediction thinking. If ants do not arrive quickly in the classroom environment, encourage students to record 'no ants came' as a valid observation and discuss why that might be.

periods.textbook_anchor: We Need Each Other — Students write a short description of their observed animal covering its name, appearance, movement, sounds, behaviour, and something surprising (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Students revisit the Write task on Textbook p. 78. Teacher reads the prompts aloud: name and describe the animal, when and where you first saw it, was it alone or with friends, its movement, sounds, eating or sleeping, something surprising or funny it did. Students think quietly about their chosen animal for a moment, then share one detail with a partner.

Students write their animal description in their notebooks. Teacher circulates with light prompts for those who are stuck: 'Close your eyes and picture it moving. What does it look like? What is it doing?' Encourage students to write freely and use their own words, including words from their home language if that helps them express something exactly. Drawings alongside the writing are welcome.

Students read their descriptions to a partner and listen to their partner's. Partners ask one question each: 'Tell me more about the sound it made' or 'What did it do that surprised you?' Students may add one more detail to their writing after hearing the question.

Three or four students share their animal story with the whole class. Teacher celebrates the range of animals chosen and the different details noticed, affirming that careful looking leads to richer knowing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present their observations of a living creature through written description and oral sharing, including details of appearance, movement, sound, and behaviour.
periods.section_context: Written description of chosen animal; name, appearance, movement, sounds, feeding, social behaviour, surprising or funny moment; sharing story with classmates.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask a student who describes something the animal did that seemed purposeful: 'Why do you think it did that?' This nudges from description toward inference without requiring formal scientific language. Accept home-language animal names and regional names warmly.

periods.activity_title: Visiting Your Plant Friend — Empathy and Mime
periods.textbook_anchor: Visiting your Plant Friend — Students play 'Guess Who I Am?' in pairs, miming an animal, bird, insect, or tree for the class to guess (p. 80)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the 'Visiting your Plant Friend' section from Textbook p. 80 aloud: the idea of going to a plant when you feel sad, happy, or angry and talking to it. Ask the class: 'Have you ever talked to a plant or an animal when you were feeling something strongly? What happened?' Let two or three students share briefly.

Teacher explains the 'Guess Who I Am?' activity from Textbook p. 80. Demonstrate by miming a slow, swaying tree in the wind, then a hopping crow, so students understand the full range — animal, bird, insect, or tree. Clarify that trees are included: students can mime branches swaying, leaves rustling, roots holding firm.

Students work in pairs. One partner whispers the name of an animal, bird, insect, or tree to the other, who then mimes it for the class. The class calls out guesses. Pairs switch roles. Teacher ensures every pair gets at least one turn as the mime. Encourage students to think about small creatures — ants, butterflies, caterpillars — not just large animals.

Class gathers and teacher asks: 'When you were pretending to be that creature, what did you notice? Was it easy or hard to imagine how it moves?' Connect to the section's message: plants and animals have their own way of being in the world, and when we pay attention, we begin to care. Read aloud the closing line from Textbook p. 80: 'Plants also need our care and support. So do animals. We can all help each other.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can use bodily mime and imaginative play to represent the characteristics of living beings and articulate empathy toward plants and animals.
periods.section_context: Visiting a plant friend when feeling sad, happy, or angry; 'Guess Who I Am?' pair mime game; animals, birds, insects, trees as mime subjects; community welcome of migratory Grey Wagtails in Valparai, Tamil Nadu.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone's family ever done something special to welcome an animal or a bird at a certain time of year — maybe feeding them, making space for a nest, or celebrating their arrival?' This draws out local traditions of welcoming nature, echoing the Valparai Grey Wagtail story, without naming it as a label.

periods.activity_title: How Should We Care? — Reflecting on Dependence
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss how they are dependent on plants and animals and how plants and animals depend on us (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 81 to the 'Let us reflect' discussion prompts. Teacher reads the three questions aloud: How are we dependent on plants and animals? How should we care for plants and animals in our environment? How do plants and animals depend on us? Students take one minute to think silently, then share their first thought with the person beside them.

Whole-class discussion. Teacher builds a two-sided web on the board: 'What we get from plants and animals' on one side, 'What plants and animals need from us' on the other. Students call out examples and teacher records them. Guide the conversation to include less obvious examples: bees pollinating flowers, earthworms aerating soil, plants cleaning the air. Ask: 'Are there animals we never care for directly but who still depend on us not to harm them?'

Students write three sentences in their notebooks: one thing they get from plants, one thing they get from animals, and one thing they personally can do to care for a plant or animal in their own life. This is their own voice, not a copy from the board.

Students share their personal action sentence with the class. Teacher closes by affirming that caring for living beings around us is something we can practise every day, in small ways, right where we are.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate specific ways humans depend on plants and animals and describe concrete actions they can take to care for living beings in their environment.
periods.section_context: Human dependence on plants and animals; plants and animals depending on humans; ways to care for plants and animals; student-chosen personal care action.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What do people in your family or neighbourhood do to look after plants or animals that they do not own?' This surfaces community-level care practices and extends the conversation beyond pet-keeping to a broader ethic of responsibility.

periods.activity_title: Sentence Frames — Expressing My Connection to Living Beings
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students complete sentence frames expressing personal connection to plants, birds, animals, and insects and identify their favourite (p. 81)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the sentence-completion task from Textbook p. 81 aloud: 'I like looking at ___ because ___. ___ make me laugh because ___. My friend ___ likes ___ because ___. I would like to take care of ___ because ___.' Students read the frames silently and think about which plants, animals, insects, or birds they want to write about.

Students complete all four sentence frames in their notebooks, then answer the follow-up questions on Textbook p. 81: Which is your favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant among those you have named? Why do you like it? Students are encouraged to use names from their home region and to write as freely as they wish — incomplete sentences or drawings alongside are welcome.

Students share their 'I would like to take care of ___ because ___' sentence with a partner and explain why they chose that creature or plant. Partners ask: 'What would you actually do to care for it?' Students add a care action to their sentence if they wish.

Four or five students share their favourite creature and their care sentence with the whole class. Teacher celebrates the diversity of choices — a moth, a drumstick tree, a stray dog — and affirms that every living being has someone who notices it and cares.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express personal connections to specific living beings through written sentence frames and articulate a reason for wanting to care for a chosen creature or plant.
periods.section_context: Sentence frames: I like looking at, make me laugh, my friend likes, I would like to take care of; favourite animal, bird, insect, or plant; reason for caring; personal care action.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students who are stuck with: 'Think of the creature you have seen most this week — even a tiny one. What do you notice about it?' Accept home-language names and regional plant names without correction, and invite students to teach the class those names.

periods.activity_title: Ranking and Drawing — Animals by Size and by Legs
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students name and draw animals, birds, and insects that have two, four, six, and eight legs (p. 82)
materials: Notebook, pencil, and crayons or coloured pencils

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking students to think of all the animals, birds, and insects they have seen or heard about through the chapter. Students call them out and teacher lists them on the board in no particular order. Then ask: 'Can we arrange these from the smallest to the largest?' Students work in pairs to draft their own ranking in their notebooks using the prompt from Textbook p. 81.

Pairs share their rankings with another pair and compare. Where they disagree, they discuss: 'Is a grasshopper smaller than a snail? Is a goat bigger than a dog?' Teacher points out that different people may have seen different sizes and that ranking requires careful observation and some knowledge. Let the disagreements stand — they are good thinking.

Students turn to Textbook p. 82 and begin the Draw task: name and draw animals, birds, and insects that have two legs, four legs, six legs, and eight legs. Students create a four-section page in their notebooks (one section per leg count) and fill each with named drawings. Teacher circulates, asking: 'Are you sure about that one? How many legs does a butterfly have? What about a spider?'

Students share one creature from their eight-legged category and one from their six-legged category with the class, since these are the less familiar groups. Teacher collects responses on the board. Close by asking: 'What do you notice about which creatures have the most legs? Do we see them near our homes?' Connect back to the chapter's opening question about who shares our living space.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify animals, birds, and insects by number of legs and sequence a set of living creatures from smallest to largest based on observation and knowledge.
periods.section_context: Ranking animals from smallest to largest; drawing and naming animals by leg count: two legs, four legs, six legs, eight legs; creatures from across the chapter including grasshopper, spider, butterfly, crow, goat, cat.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of a creature with no legs at all? Where does it fit?' This extends the classification naturally. If students disagree on the size ranking, encourage them to explain their reasoning — the quality of the thinking matters more than arriving at a single correct order.

assessment_items.question_text: Shirin noticed that pigeons often come to her kitchen windowsill even though her family never invited them. Which is the most likely reason the pigeons come?

options.label: A
options.text: They come to eat the potted plants inside the kitchen.

options.label: B
options.text: They find food, shelter, or warmth near the window.

options.label: C
options.text: They only come because Shirin called them by name.

options.label: D
options.text: They were sent by another family to deliver a message.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This item tests whether students can apply the idea that uninvited animals enter homes in search of basic needs — food, shelter, warmth — rather than through human invitation or magical thinking.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the animals, birds, insects, and plants that share their living space and explain why some arrive uninvited.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates a fanciful or magical explanation; student has not connected the animal's behaviour to its biological needs.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows a self-centred view — that animals respond only to direct human action; does not reflect the chapter's idea of animals acting on their own needs.
what_each_option_reveals.A: A plausible-sounding distractor but confuses invited plants (potted) with the pigeon's motivation; student may be recalling the opening picture without applying the concept of need.

assessment_items.task: Think of an animal, bird, or insect that sometimes comes to your home and that you do not particularly like. Draw or write about it. Then write or say: 'One kind thing I could do (or not do) when I see it is ___.'
assessment_items.scaffold: 1. Name or draw the creature. 2. Write one word for how it makes you feel. 3. Write or say: 'One kind thing I could do (or not do) when I see it is ___.'
format_of_output: A name or drawing of the creature
One sentence about a kind response
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any uninvited creature the student names — lizard, cockroach, moth, crow, ant — and any genuine kind response (leaving it alone, gently putting it outside, not harming it). There is no single correct creature or action. The item assesses whether the student can identify a compassionate alternative to harm.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate their feelings toward uninvited living beings and reflect on compassionate responses rather than harm.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can hold a negative feeling (dislike, fear) and still choose a non-harmful response — demonstrating the disposition of compassion toward all living beings.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Part 1 anchors the response in something real from the student's experience. Part 2 validates honest feeling. Part 3 is the core demonstration: the student must propose a behaviour, not just a feeling.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific creature, acknowledges real feeling, proposes a concrete kind action (e.g., 'I will gently move it outside' or 'I will leave it alone'). Weak: says 'I don't know' for the kind action, or proposes harm as the response.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write may draw the creature and act out their kind response for the teacher. Students may respond in their home language.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written and/or drawn response with an oral sharing option
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A low-barrier format ensures all students can access the task regardless of writing fluency; the emotional dimension is better expressed through choice of format than forced writing.

assessment_items.question_text: Shambhu's father explained that when a monkey eats a mango and throws away the seed, something important happens. (a) What happens to the seed? (b) Name one other way that animals help plants grow or spread.
expected_elements: A new mango plant can grow from the seed the monkey threw away.

One additional example of animals helping plants — e.g., squirrels bury and forget nuts so new plants grow; bees carry pollen from flower to flower; birds drop seeds in new places through their droppings.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for part (a) if the student conveys that the seed can grow into a new plant. For part (b), accept any plausible animal–plant helping relationship from the chapter or from the student's own knowledge. Regional examples (e.g., a specific local bird dispersing seeds) are correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how plants and animals depend on each other and on humans, using examples from their own environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Part (a): The seed can grow into a new mango plant / tree (seed dispersal).
Part (b): Any one example of an animal helping a plant — squirrel burying nuts, bees pollinating flowers, birds spreading seeds through droppings, animal waste making soil fertile.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajan chose to observe a crow for the 'Get to Know an Animal' activity. Which of the following is the BEST thing he could write down in his observation notebook?

options.label: A
options.text: Crows are black birds that are found all over India.

options.label: B
options.text: I think crows are scary and I don't like them.

options.label: C
options.text: The crow is the state bird of some Indian states.

options.label: D
options.text: The crow made a loud cawing sound and flew to a nearby branch when a dog came close.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This item checks whether students understand that observation recording should capture specific, witnessed behaviours — sound, movement, response to events — rather than general knowledge, opinion, or facts from other sources.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a familiar animal closely and record its behaviour, movement, sounds, and social habits using a structured frame.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student is recalling general knowledge rather than personal, direct observation — confuses knowing about with observing.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student is recording personal feeling, not observed behaviour; has not grasped the purpose of an observation notebook.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student is drawing on outside factual information, not on what they personally saw — shows a tendency to look up rather than look at.

assessment_items.question_text: In the Busy Ants experiment, Priya placed sugar, papad, and chapati on the floor. Before the ants arrived, she made a guess. (a) Write ONE guess Priya might have made before the experiment. (b) After watching, Priya found that most ants went to the sugar. Was her guess right or wrong? How do you know?
expected_elements: A clear prediction stated before observing — e.g., 'I think the ants will go to the sweet food first' or 'I think ants will like the chapati best.'
A comparison between the prediction and the observation — states whether the guess matched what actually happened and gives the observation as evidence (most ants went to sugar).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any reasonable prior prediction for part (a). For part (b), credit responses that clearly distinguish between what was predicted and what was observed, and use the observation as evidence for the conclusion. The student does not need to use formal scientific vocabulary.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can set up a simple inquiry, make predictions, record observations, and compare results to their predictions.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Part (a): Any stated prediction about which food the ants would prefer, how many would come, where they would come from, or whether they would all look the same.
Part (b): A judgment (right/wrong/partly right) supported by the observation that most ants went to the sugar; shows the student can compare a prior belief to evidence.

assessment_items.task: Write a short description (four to six sentences, or a drawing with labels) of an animal, bird, or insect you have seen. Include: what it looks like, how it moves, what sounds it makes, and one thing it did that surprised you or made you curious.
assessment_items.scaffold:
1. Name of the animal / bird / insect: ___
2. What it looks like: ___
3. How it moves: ___
4. Sounds it makes: ___
5. Something surprising or funny it did: ___
format_of_output: Written description of four to six sentences OR labelled drawing
Must include appearance, movement, sound, and one surprising detail
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any animal, bird, or insect the student has actually seen. Regional or local creatures are equally valid. Award credit for specificity in any two or more of the four dimensions (appearance, movement, sound, surprise) — a response that covers all four with even one detail each is strong. Note: regionally varied animals and behaviours are expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present their observations of a living creature through written description and oral sharing, including details of appearance, movement, sound, and behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate direct observation into a communicable description, capturing specific sensory details rather than general facts.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each numbered line targets one dimension of observation. A student who completes all five lines meets the full implied_lo. A student who completes any three of the five still demonstrates meaningful observational writing.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific details ('its wings made a clicking sound', 'it tilted its head sideways before pecking'). Weak: generic statements ('it is an animal', 'it eats food') or copied textbook descriptions without personal observation.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may produce a labelled drawing in place of written sentences. Students may write in their home language. Oral dictation to the teacher is acceptable for students with writing difficulties.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The dual format option ensures students who express themselves better through visual means can still demonstrate the same observational competency.

assessment_items.task: Choose a plant, animal, bird, or insect. Think about how it feels and what it needs — just like you have feelings and needs. Act out or draw: (a) what you think it feels when it is happy, and (b) what it needs from you or from the world around it.
assessment_items.scaffold:
1. I chose: ___
2. When it is happy, it might: ___ (act this out OR draw it)
3. What it needs is: ___
4. One thing I can do to help it: ___
format_of_output: Name or drawing of chosen living being
An acted-out or drawn expression of the creature's happiness
A statement of what it needs
One action the student can take
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any living being from the chapter or from the student's own experience. There is no single correct answer for what a plant or animal 'feels' — credit imaginative, empathetic responses. The key demonstration is that the student attributes needs and a form of wellbeing to a non-human living being and connects that to a personal action.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use bodily mime and imaginative play to represent the characteristics of living beings and articulate empathy toward plants and animals.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can project empathy onto a non-human living being and articulate the relationship as reciprocal — the living being has needs, and the student has a role in meeting them.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Parts 1 and 2 build imaginative engagement. Part 3 moves to concrete ecological knowledge (what does this creature actually need?). Part 4 is the behavioural commitment — the student moves from empathy to action.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific creature, imaginative and detailed representation of happiness, realistic need (water, food, space, quiet), and a concrete personal action. Weak: generic ('it feels happy', 'it needs food') without specificity or personal connection.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Acting out (mime) is the primary mode and does not require writing. Students who prefer to draw may draw all four parts. Students may respond in their home language.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Mime performance and/or drawing with oral explanation
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Mime was the core activity of the unit; this format continues that mode of expression while adding a reflective layer, ensuring continuity with the learning experience.

assessment_items.question_text: Leela says: 'Plants and animals don't really need us. They were here before humans and they can manage on their own.' Do you agree or disagree with Leela? Give at least two reasons to support your view, using examples of plants or animals you know.
look_for: A clear position (agree or disagree) stated at the start.

At least two reasons supported by examples — e.g., humans have changed environments so much that many animals now depend on human protection or care; some plants in cities only survive because humans water them; on the other hand, the student might thoughtfully agree that wild plants and animals manage without humans, but nuance this by noting the chapter's examples of mutual care.
Use of specific examples from the chapter or from the student's own experience (not vague generalisations).
Recognition that the relationship between humans and living beings involves responsibility, not just dependence.
assessment_items.annotation: Both 'agree' and 'disagree' positions are acceptable if well-reasoned. Credit the quality of reasoning and the use of specific examples over the direction of the argument. A student who agrees with Leela but acknowledges that humans have a responsibility not to harm is demonstrating the same core competency as one who disagrees.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate specific ways humans depend on plants and animals and describe concrete actions they can take to care for living beings in their environment.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

look_for: A clear stance on the question stated at the outset.
At least two distinct reasons, each supported by a named example (not generic).
Engagement with the idea of mutual dependence — even if the student agrees with Leela, they should acknowledge that humans and living beings affect each other.
A sense of human responsibility toward living beings, even if expressed simply.

assessment_items.task:
Complete these four sentences with the names of real plants, animals, birds, or insects that you know. Then choose the one you love most and write two sentences about why you would like to take care of it.

a. I like looking at ___ because ___.
b. ___ make(s) me laugh because ___.
c. My friend ___ likes ___ because ___.
d. I would like to take care of ___ because ___.

Now write: My favourite is ___, and I will take care of it by ___.
assessment_items.scaffold: Fill in all four sentence frames. Then add your two sentences about your favourite creature or plant.
format_of_output: Two additional sentences naming the favourite and describing a care action
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any real plant, animal, bird, or insect the student names. Regional plants and creatures — including ones not mentioned in the textbook — are equally valid. The care action in the final sentence must be concrete and feasible (watering a plant, leaving food, not disturbing a nest). Note: regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express personal connections to specific living beings through written sentence frames and articulate a reason for wanting to care for a chosen creature or plant.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can name specific living beings they have a personal relationship with and move from emotional connection to a stated intention to care — demonstrating the disposition of responsibility toward the natural world.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The four frames build from observation (looking), emotion (laughing), social sharing (friend's choice), and finally care intention. The final two sentences consolidate the disposition by requiring a concrete action.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific named creatures with genuine reasons ('I like looking at a kingfisher because its colours surprise me every time'); care action is concrete and doable. Weak: blank frames, generic creatures ('an animal'), or care action that is vague ('I will be good to it').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may name creatures in their home language; accept all regional names. Students who cannot write may dictate their sentences to the teacher or a peer. Drawings alongside the sentences are welcome.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written sentence frames with an oral option
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Sentence frames lower the writing barrier while maintaining linguistic expression of personal connection — a mode well suited to the empathy-focused chapter close.

assessment_items.question_text: Kavya is sorting animals into groups by the number of legs they have. She places a butterfly, a grasshopper, and a beetle together. Which is the correct group name for these creatures?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. Butterfly, grasshopper, and beetle are all insects with six legs. This item tests the classification skill developed in the drawing task, specifically the six-legged category which students often find less familiar than two or four.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify animals, birds, and insects by number of legs and sequence a set of living creatures from smallest to largest based on observation and knowledge.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has confused insects with four-legged animals (mammals); may be thinking of common pets rather than applying the leg-count classification.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student is thinking of spiders (eight legs) — a confusion between the eight-legged and six-legged categories, suggesting the two groups were not clearly distinguished during the drawing task.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be thinking of birds (two-legged) and confusing flight ability with number of legs, since all three creatures can fly.
